analysis.one_liner: Strips presidential approval for cross-border oil, gas, and power lines and sets a 120-day decision deadline.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 238-173 on June 24, 2014, but the Senate never voted before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would overhaul how pipelines and power lines that cross into Canada or Mexico get approved. It would eliminate the requirement for a presidential permit, replace it with a new 'certificate of crossing' that officials must issue within 120 days after environmental review is finished unless they find the project is not in the public interest, and it would repeal the requirement for a federal order before natural gas or electricity is traded with Canada and Mexico. The House passed it, largely along party lines, but the Senate never took it up before the two-year Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that build and operate cross-border oil pipelines, natural gas export projects, and electric transmission lines. They would get a mandatory 120-day decision clock, lose the presidential-permit gate that today gives the administration final say, and no longer need a federal order to move gas or electricity across the northern or southern border. Existing lines would be grandfathered: even a flow reversal, volume expansion, or change of ownership would require no new approval.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the discretionary presidential permit with a certificate of crossing that the Secretary of State (for oil pipelines) or Secretary of Energy (for power lines) must issue within 120 days after environmental review concludes, unless the project is found not to be in the U.S. public interest.
Declares that no presidential permit is necessary at all for any cross-border oil or gas pipeline or electric transmission facility.

Repeals the Federal Power Act requirement that electricity exports to foreign countries get prior federal authorization, and amends the Natural Gas Act so no federal order is required to import or export natural gas to or from Canada or Mexico.

Retains environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act before the certificate clock starts, keeps reliability standards for transmission facilities, and keeps Natural Gas Act requirements for the siting and operation of import/export facilities.

analysis.who_pays: People who live along proposed cross-border pipeline and transmission routes, and the public more broadly, would lose the executive-level check that currently weighs foreign-policy, environmental, and community concerns before a project crosses the border. The mandatory 120-day deadline and the 'must-issue-unless' standard tilt the process toward approval. Domestic natural gas consumers could face a weaker backstop against export-driven price pressure, since no federal order would be needed to ship gas to Canada or Mexico.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near pipeline routes and federal oversight

drawbacks.text: No presidential permit would be required for any cross-border pipeline or transmission facility, eliminating the executive review process that applies under existing executive orders.

The certificate must be issued within 120 days after environmental review ends unless officials affirmatively find the project is not in the public interest — a 'must-issue' default that shifts the burden onto opponents.

Modifications to existing cross-border lines — including reversing the flow direction, expanding volume, changing ownership, or adding interconnections — would need no new certificate or permit at all.

The version originally introduced would have declared approvals not to be 'major federal action' under the National Environmental Policy Act, sidestepping environmental review; that language was revised in committee before the floor vote.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would genuinely speed up permitting for cross-border energy projects, which could mean faster construction and, in the case of electricity transmission, potentially more imports such as Canadian power. But its main effect is to remove a discretionary public check on major fossil-fuel infrastructure decisions — the presidential permit — and replace it with a deadline-driven, must-issue process, while grandfathering expansions of existing lines with no review at all. The bill was debated in the shadow of the delayed Keystone XL pipeline approval, and its design is best understood as a response to that delay. The speed benefit is real; the loss of oversight is the larger and more permanent change.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 238-173 on June 24, 2014, but after the Senate read it twice and put it on its calendar, no vote ever came before that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Fred Upton introduced the bill on October 22, 2013; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Natural Resources Committees.
The Energy and Commerce Committee ordered it reported as amended on a 31-19 vote on May 8, 2014, and the other two committees were discharged so the bill could move to the floor.
A rule (H. Res. 636) confined floor debate to one hour and limited amendments to three Democratic proposals, each of which the chair announced had failed.

Rep. Brad Schneider's motion to recommit — instructing the committee to add protections for the Great Lakes and drinking water — failed 185-227, with all 223 voting Republicans opposed and 185 Democrats in favor.
Final passage passed 238-173, with 221 of 232 Republicans voting yes and only 17 of 199 Democrats joining them.
The Senate received the bill on June 25, 2014, read it twice, and placed it on its calendar under General Orders, where it remained with no further action through the end of the 113th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the existing presidential-permit process and federal checks on cross-border energy projects stayed in place, and the pipeline developers, natural gas exporters, and utilities that sought streamlined approvals did not get them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing permitting rules and their backers

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: 221 of 232 Republicans voted yes while only 17 of 199 Democrats did, and the Democratic motion to recommit drew 185 Democratic votes and zero Republican votes.

industries.industry: Cross-border oil and gas pipeline developers
industries.note: The bill would replace the discretionary presidential permit with a mandatory 120-day certificate process and declare no presidential permit necessary at all, removing the administration's ability to delay or reject projects. Faster permitting could mean cheaper energy infrastructure, but the public cost is the loss of an executive-level review of foreign-policy and environmental concerns.

No federal order would be required to import or export natural gas to or from Canada or Mexico, removing a public-interest determination before gas leaves the country. A weaker export check can tighten domestic supply and put upward pressure on prices for home heating and electricity.

The bill repeals the requirement for federal authorization before electricity is exported to foreign countries, though it imposes reliability standards on cross-border segments. Faster cross-border transmission could enable imports such as Canadian power, but it strips a public-interest gate on exports.
